The DPA found that Google LLC and Google Ireland Ltd. are joint controllers for the processing of personal data in connection with Google services in the EEA.

The Irish DPC announced two final decisions against Meta Platforms Ireland following own-volition inquiries into a 2018 breach in which attackers exploited Facebook user tokens, affecting about 29 million accounts globally (about 3 million in the EU/EEA). The DPC found infringements of Articles 33(3), 33(5), 25(1) and 25(2) GDPR, issued reprimands and ordered administrative fines totalling €251 million. The individual fines were €8 million, €3 million, €130 million and €110 million. No objections were raised to the draft decision under the Article 60 cooperation procedure.

The DPA fined a loan comparison service provider €950,000 for making loan applications available to the public without implementing appropriate safeguards, thus violating the principle of integrity and confidentiality.

A Belgian hospital notified the DPA of a ransomware attack in 2021 that made systems, medical records and emergency care unavailable for days. After an inspection, the Litigation Chamber found failures in security measures, no data protection impact assessment, and breaches of integrity and confidentiality and accountability. It fined the hospital EUR 200,000 after reducing a starting amount for the hospital's financial difficulties, the COVID context and the energy crisis, and ordered compliance measures within 90 days. The Market Court on 3 September 2025 partly annulled the decision and cut the fine to EUR 50,000; the DPA has appealed in cassation.
The DPA fined a newspaper €10,000 for failing to make use of anonymization techniques in order to minimise the personal data shown in a video that was part of an online article.
The EDPS issued a reprimand to the European Commission for unlawfully targeting X users based on their political views in order to promote a legislative proposal.
The DPA issued a reprimand to a hospital trust for failing to adequately track data access requests and for not responding to approximately 32% of those requests in due time.
A user repeatedly failed to unsubscribe from a newsletter despite confirmation from the controller. NAIH found the company violated Articles 6(1)(a), 12(3), and 25(1) GDPR.
The DPA fined a Public Transport Company RON 19,902 (€4,006) as it had made video recordings of its employees at work for several years.
The DPA issued a warning to a media company after it failed to adequately answer to and comply with an erasure request for more than a year, thus violating Article 12 GDPR and Article 17 GDPR
The DPA fined a controller €2,000 for sending nude pictures he had taken of the data subject to his own phone and storing them on it until the data subject noticed and demanded their erasure.

A patient complained that photos of her face, taken before and after an aesthetic surgery procedure, were published on a doctor's Instagram profile without her consent. The doctor said a former social media manager posted them and that consent forms lacked a publication clause; the photos had been removed and a civil settlement reached. The Garante found the dissemination of health data unlawful under Articles 5 and 9 GDPR and Article 2-septies(8) of the Code, rated the gravity as high, and fined the doctor EUR 20,000. No corrective measures were ordered because the photos were already deleted.
A bank was fined €3,500,000 for failing to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures after customers were given access to accounts they were not authorised to access.

Several citizens reported that the municipality of Portici used red-light cameras to detect traffic offences without any information signs near them. The Garante found that, from start-up until after its inquiry began, the municipality gave no first- or second-level information to data subjects and had not carried out a data protection impact assessment before starting the processing. The municipality had wrongly believed these steps were not required and fixed them once the inquiry started. The Garante found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a), 12, 13 and 35 GDPR and imposed a single fine of EUR 6,000, with publication of the order.

A former employee of the municipality of Corte Franca complained that a council resolution recording his resignation, qualification, office, hours worked and last working day had been published online and was findable through search engines. The Garante found there was no legal basis for this dissemination, contrary to Articles 5 and 6 GDPR and Article 2-ter of the Italian Code. The municipality had also communicated its DPO's contact details to the authority late, breaching Article 37(7). For the dissemination the Garante imposed a fine of EUR 6,000. For the late DPO communication it only issued a reprimand, treating it as a minor violation by a small municipality. The decision is to be published on the Garante's website.

A man complained that he kept receiving promotional emails and SMS from the website docenti.it, run by Start To Fly S.r.l., for years despite repeatedly unsubscribing and asking to be deleted. The company said it was an error caused by re-uploading an old mailing list and invoked legitimate interest and the soft-spam exception. The Garante rejected this: the only legal basis for such messages is consent, which had been withdrawn, and the deletion request was ignored. It found violations of Articles 6(1)(a) and 17 GDPR and Article 130(2) of the Code, banned promotional processing without documented consent, and fined the company EUR 10,000.

A tenant complained about extensive camera surveillance in a residential building in Malmö run by the landlord company and about missing information. IMY found that the company had no legal basis for the surveillance (Article 6(1)) apart from the garage, and that its signs lacked the controller's identity and contact details (Article 13). IMY imposed an administrative fine of SEK 200,000, treating the infringements as low severity and negligent, and ordered the company to stop surveillance of all places except the garage and to add identity and contact details to the signs within four weeks of the decision becoming final.
Additionally, the DPA fined a medical center RON 10,000 (€4,972) as it forced users to accept cookies to access its website. These cookies collected and stored personal data of the data subject.
The DPA fined an insurance company €4,000,000 after an unauthorised third party was able to access the data of over 25,000 former clients of the controller due to inadequate security measures.

The DPA ordered a doctor to rephrase their consent form as the purpose of promoting the doctor's services on social media was not clearly listed for the processing of data subjects’ pictures. Such processing without valid consent was deemed unlawful.
The DPA fined a controller €20,000 for failing to respond to the data subject’s multiple requests to discontinue the delivery of advertising emails.

KASPR runs a Chrome extension that shows professional phone numbers and emails of people whose LinkedIn profiles users visit, drawing on a database of about 160 million contacts. Following several complaints, the CNIL inspected the company in July 2022. The restricted committee found breaches of the lawful basis requirement (Art. 6), storage limitation (Art. 5(1)(e)), transparency (Arts. 12 and 14) and the right of access (Art. 15). In particular, it found that contacts who had limited the visibility of their details on LinkedIn were collected through synchronisation of users' accounts. It imposed a EUR 240,000 fine, a compliance injunction with a EUR 10,000 per day penalty after six months, and publication of the decision, anonymised after two years.

The ICO issued a £120,000 penalty to Money Bubble Ltd, having determined MBL made unsolicited calls for the purposes of marketing and contravened section SSA of the Data Protection Act and regulations 21 and 24 of the PECR.

A Spanish financial institution was fined €500,000 for failing to ensure the confidentiality and security of customer data under Article 5.1(f) GDPR. A cyberattack exposed sensitive data due to inadequate security measures, violating Article 32 GDPR.

The DPA reprimanded a tech company for the centralised storage and disclosure of end-customers’ data to different retail companies. This practice violated the principles of data minimization, storage limitation, accountability, as well as data protection by default and by design.

The Region of Molise notified a personal data breach in its regional electronic health record portal: a logged-in patient manipulated a URL and could search and view data and health documents of other citizens (7 people affected). The Garante opened proceedings against the region and also against Molise Dati S.p.A., its processor responsible for technical implementation and security. It found that Molise Dati failed to put in place security measures appropriate to the risk, in breach of Article 32 GDPR. Considering the gravity low and noting its cooperation and quick remediation, it fined the company EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

The Molise Region notified the Garante of a data breach in its regional electronic health record portal: a logged-in patient changed a URL and reached a search function reserved for doctors, which let them view the health records of 7 other people. The Garante found that the Region, as controller, had breached the integrity and confidentiality principle, data protection by design and security obligations. It treated the gravity as low, noted the Region's high cooperation and quick fix, and imposed a fine of EUR 10,000. Publication of the order was also ordered.

The Molise Region notified a personal data breach in its regional electronic health record portal: a logged-in user with the patient role could manipulate a URL and search and view the data of other citizens, affecting 7 people. The flaw was a coding error by Engineering Ingegneria Informatica S.p.A., which designed and built the system as a further sub-processor. The Garante found that Engineering had not put in place adequate security measures and had not tested them properly, in breach of Article 32 GDPR. It fined the company EUR 10,000, treating the gravity as low and noting its high cooperation, and ordered publication of the decision.

The Italian DPA examined two complaints against the energy supplier E.ON Energia. One complainant received telemarketing calls based on a Facebook contact form she never filled in and got no answer to her access request; the other had her marketing consents recorded wrongly in the CRM and kept receiving promotional calls. The Garante found breaches of lawfulness and accountability, of the rules on authorising and supervising staff and processors, and of the rules on handling data subject rights. It fined E.ON EUR 892,738, banned further processing of the complainants' data, ordered updating of staff authorisation forms and ordered publication of the decision.

The DPA reprimanded a security company for a lack of appropriate technical and organisational measures, especially the insufficient storage of log data, that made it unfeasible to trace any misuse of personal data.

The DPA ordered a school to bring its use of CCTV surveillance into compliance by providing more detailed information to data subjects, and by taking other steps to ensure transparency, security, and the minimisation of the processing of personal data.

A patient's anaesthesia questionnaire, containing another patient's name, PESEL number and health data, was handed to an unauthorised person. The hospital did not notify the Polish DPA within 72 hours and its notice to the affected patient lacked a description of the measures taken or proposed to remedy the breach. The President of UODO found violations of Articles 33(1) and 34(1)-(2) GDPR, fined the hospital PLN 29,684.04 (EUR 6,800) and ordered it to notify the affected person properly within 3 days. The fine was calculated under EDPB Guidelines 04/2022 with a low-seriousness starting point, adjusted for turnover and reduced for net mitigating factors.

The Dutch DPA fined Netflix International B.V. EUR 4,750,000 for not informing its customers clearly enough, both in its privacy statement and in replies to access requests. The gaps concerned purposes and legal bases, recipients, retention periods and international transfers. The case began with complaints filed by NOYB for two data subjects with the Austrian authority, which passed them to the AP. The AP treated this as two separate infringing acts, set the starting amount at EUR 2.5 million each, and found the seriousness low. It lowered the amount because Netflix cooperated, handled the complainants' requests, fixed the recipients part quickly and the case took very long.

The Belgian DPA imposed a fine of 5 000 € for failing to uphold the right to object of a data subject by irregularly processing personal data and failing its obligation of ensuring data protection measures by default and design.

The DPA fined a university €40,000 for failing to implement adequate security measures and not notifying them in time of a data breach after a compromised email account resulted in an employee falling victim to financial fraud.

After two online inspections of the orange.fr site and the Mail Orange email service in 2023, the CNIL restricted committee found that ORANGE SA breached Article L. 34-5 of the postal and electronic communications code, by displaying advertisements between emails without consent, and Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act, because cookies continued to be read after consent was withdrawn. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 50 million. It also ordered the company to make the withdrawal of consent effective, with a daily penalty of EUR 100,000 after three months. The decision is published, and the company will no longer be named after two years.

The DPA fined Illumia, an energy provider, €678,897 for its aggressive telemarketing operations which lacked a valid legal basis. Moreover, Illumia fully outsourced the activity to processors without having a processing agreement.

The Italian DPA fined Foodinho, a Glovo group company, EUR 5 million for unlawfully processing the personal data of over 35,000 riders through its digital platform. The investigation found that account deactivation messages did not tell riders they could contest the decision, that automated systems (excellence score, order assignment) lacked human intervention and contestation safeguards, and that data including geolocation were sent to third parties without informing riders, even outside working hours. The Garante issued specific orders, banned further processing of biometric facial recognition data used for identity checks, and required changes to messages, GPS indicators and reputation mechanisms. This text is a press release, not the decision itself.
The DPA issued a €2,400,000 fine to the Finnish postal service for automatically creating an electronic mailbox for its customers without their consent and without an option to opt-out.
The DPA fined a County Council €29,500 for the excessive processing of CCTV footage of public and private areas and the failure to conduct a Data Protection Impact Assessment.
The DPA held that, under Italian law, the consent of both parents is needed in order to share the picture of a child on a social network.
The DPA fined a Health Agency €8,000 for unlawfully publishing the names of candidates who were rejected during a public job selection procedure.

The Italian supervisory authority investigated the cookie practices of an ecommerce website. The data controller addressed the authority’s concerns during the investigation. The authority issued a warning.

A website selling clothes and beauty products had a cookie banner, which linked to a privacy policy that could be edited by every visitor. Moreover, no cookie policy was present in the website, in violation of several GDPR articles.
The DPA ordered Google to remove search results showing outdated and inaccurate information about a criminal proceeding against the data subject.

After an earlier decision (16/2022) fining the dating agency 'ANOIXIS' EUR 54,000, the authority received 15 new complaints about unsolicited marketing SMS sent without consent or any prior relationship. The authority traced the sending number and the website domain to the sole trader running the business. The controller never answered the authority's requests for views and did not attend the hearing. The authority found breaches of Article 11 of Law 3471/2006 and Article 31 GDPR, noted no compliance with the earlier decision, and imposed a fine of EUR 45,000. It also asked the telecoms regulator EETT to check the domain registration and consider deleting the domain name.
The DPA held that the erasure of all personal data from a former employee’s work phone by the employer was unlawful since it was not limited to corporate information.

The Hamburg DPA ran a sector-wide audit of major debt collection companies. On site it found that one company had kept a six-digit number of records with personal data after the retention periods had expired, in some cases up to five years, with no legal basis. The data was not passed to third parties in that time. The authority imposed a fine of EUR 900,000. The company admitted the violation and accepted the fine, and its cooperation was taken into account. A similar procedure against another audited company is still ongoing.

The DPA fined the operator of a website €350.000 (PLN 1,527,855) and its processor €4.590 (PLN 20,037) for data security violations after a configuration error on the website led to a data breach concerning 21,453 individuals

The DPA fined a postal service provider €200,000 for failing to implement measures which would have prevented thousands of letters being abandoned in fields and a river. Furthermore, the controller was ordered to implement a tracking system.
The DPA fined a controller €1,400 for not complying with an Article 15 GDPR access request and for failing to cooperate with the DPA, thus violating Article 31 GDPR.

The DPA fined OpenAI €15,000,000 for the non-transparent processing of personal data without correctly identifying an adequate legal basis. It also mandated a six-month public campaign to raise awareness about ChatGPT’s data processing practices and user rights under the GDPR.
After a data breach concerning more than 3,500 data subjects, the DPA ordered Intesa Sanpaolo bank to notify the affected data subjects pursuant to Article 34 GDPR.

A former EYP employee complained that the National Intelligence Service sent lists with her name, university education and staff category to the Ministers and the Police Chief one day before the law on transferring staff to the Police entered into force. The Authority found there was no legal basis for the disclosure, that the lawfulness principle was breached, and that the controller had not shown it informed the data subject under Article 13. It fined EYP EUR 5,000 in total, EUR 4,000 for Article 5(1)(a) and EUR 1,000 for Article 13. It treated the breach as negligent, not intentional, and found no material damage.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation of Untold SRL in September 2024. It found that the controller never answered a data subject's access request and did not handle an erasure request within the legal time limits. It imposed two fines, EUR 10,000 for the access breach and EUR 5,000 for the erasure breach, and ordered the controller to answer the access request and to put in place measures and staff training so that data subject requests are handled correctly and on time.

The DPA ordered the public broadcaster to adjust its news website’s cookie banner since the graphic emphasis of the "accept all cookies" option invalidates the data subject’s consent Article 6(1)(a) GDPR.
The DPA issued a reprimand to a controller for further processing and sharing data collected via cookies which were placed by the controller without the users' consent.

The Romanian authority concluded an investigation into Vodafone România in September 2024. A data subject complained that several email addresses, including their own, were disclosed when messages about a change of account manager were sent to business clients' representatives without hiding the recipients. The authority found Article 32 GDPR was breached because insufficient technical and organisational measures protected confidentiality. It fined the company 24,870.5 lei (about EUR 5,000) and ordered a reassessment of security measures, especially staff training and regular checks that instructions are followed.
The DPA dismissed the complaint related an employee´s depiction in brochures, mailings and training sessions of their former employer.

The Irish DPC announced its final decision on LinkedIn Ireland after a complaint-based inquiry into processing of members' data for behavioural analysis and targeted advertising. It found LinkedIn lacked a valid legal basis (consent, legitimate interests, contractual necessity), breached transparency duties and the fairness principle. The DPC issued a reprimand, an order to bring processing into compliance, and three administrative fines totalling EUR 310 million. The draft decision went through Article 60 cooperation with no objections.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation into Profi Rom Food in September 2024. It found the company sent copies of several employees' identity cards to a service provider without a legal basis, and fined it RON 49,744 (EUR 10,000) for breaching Articles 5(1)(a), 5(2) and 6(1). Separately, after a breach notification, an employee filmed a company monitor with a personal phone and the videos were shared on WhatsApp, which led to a warning under Article 32. Corrective measures were ordered on lawful processing, access to video recordings and regular staff training.
The DPA fined a bank €180,000 for accessing the data of a former customer more than 47 times without any legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR after the contractual relationship had ended.

Grue municipality notified a personal data breach: documents about pupils' school-environment decisions (9A decisions), with names, birth dates, some national ID numbers and parents' contact details, were published on the public mail log for about three weeks, and eight further similar cases were found back to 2020. The cause was human error and weaknesses in the archive system. Datatilsynet found that the municipality had not implemented adequate technical and organisational measures for confidentiality, and had published personal data, including special categories, without a legal basis. It imposed an administrative fine of NOK 250,000, reduced from the NOK 400,000 announced in the notice after considering the municipality's size and poor finances.

The DPA held that an insurance company had not violated the requirements of Article 12(1) GDPR and Article 15(3) GDPR by first providing the data subject with a written transcript of the call recording, rather than the call recording itself.
“The DPA fined Raiffeisen Bank RON 99,466 (€20,000) after inadequate technical and organisational measures allowed for the misuse of customers’ accounts and personal data by the bank’s employees

The President of UODO learned from a private message that a public authority had no data protection officer. After requesting explanations, he found that no DPO had been formally designated from 25 May 2018 until March 2024, and that the DPO's contact details were not published or notified to the supervisory authority. He found infringements of Article 37(1)(a) and 37(7) GDPR, regarded as intentional, and fined the authority PLN 25,000. He also ordered it to publish the DPO's contact details within 7 days.
The DPA fined a municipality €8,000 for unlawfully publishing personal and sensitive data related to the termination of the data subject's employment.

A debtor complained that debt-collection company Serfin 97 S.r.l. used an email address belonging to an acquaintance to chase a debt. Serfin was acting as processor (sub-servicer) for the securitisation vehicle P.E.S. S.r.l. The Garante found that Serfin had added contact data on its own without recording the source or passing it to the controller, breaching the processor obligations of Article 28(3)(a), (e) and (h). Because Serfin had already deleted the address and adopted new technical and organisational measures, no corrective measures were ordered, but a fine of EUR 60,000 was imposed and the decision is to be published.
The Italian supervisory authority warned a company over the cookie practices of its ecommerce website. The company voluntarily took its website offline during the investigation.

The ICO issued a reprimand to Southend-on-Sea City Council, in Essex, after hidden data on a spreadsheet released as part of a freedom of information request revealed the sensitive personal details of staff, violating Article 5 GDPR.

The DPA found that publishing personal data of property owners in an effort to compile publicly available property information cannot be based on legitimate interest within the meaning of Article 6(1)(f) GDPR.
The DPA issued a €5,000 fine to a controller for designating the managing director of the company as the DPO, therefore creating a conflict of interest in violation of Article 38(6) GDPR.

The DPA affirmed a controller’s legitimate interest to cross-check a caller’s phone number with their customer database in order to identify a calling customer. The legitimate interest also covered sending a survey to the data subject after the call.

The DPA dismissed a tenant’s complaint against the processing of their divorce status by their former landlord. The DPA held that the complaint was manifestly unfounded and excessive under Article 57(4) GDPR.

The DPA reprimanded a media company for failing to implement an option to reject cookies on the first layer of the cookie banner on one of its websites. Also, the option to accept all cookies was unlawfully highlighted in a catchy colour.

The DPA fined a controller PLN 353,589 (€82,000) after insufficient security measures allowed for a ransomware attack encrypting data of approximately 200 customers and employees. An involved processor was fined PLN 9,822 (€2,200).

The DPA fined a controller €5,000 for unlawfully publishing an employee’s image and personal data on the company’s website. Posing for a picture and providing data from a CV did not meet the consent requirements under Article 4(11) GDPR.

The DPA reprimanded an insurance company after it placed cookies without the data subject's consent and unlawfully transferred data to the USA through the use of Google Analytics in violation of Chapter V of the GDPR.

The DPA fined a company managing a zoo and water park €250,000 for unlawfully implementing a mandatory fingerprint identification system in its parks. Data subjects with promotional tickets allowing access to both parks with one ticket were required to provide their fingerprint data.
The DPA fined a controller €200,000 for failing to ensure a level of security appropriate to the large-scale processing of sensitive medical data, therefore violating Article 32 GDPR.

The DPA fined a hotel €1,200 for breaching Article 5(1)(c) GDPR by retaining copies of travellers' IDs. The hotel was ordered to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures, i.e. to remove the requirement to provide an ID and to delete IDs already on file.

The Irish DPC announced its final decision on an inquiry opened in April 2019 after Meta Platforms Ireland notified it that it had accidentally stored some users' passwords in plaintext on internal systems. The DPC found infringements of Articles 33(1), 33(5), 5(1)(f) and 32(1) GDPR. It issued a reprimand and administrative fines totalling €91 million. The draft decision was circulated to other supervisory authorities under Article 60 and no objections were raised.
The DPA fined an optician €20,000 for sending a former customer a marketing email even though she had expressly objected to this form of processing.

The DPA ordered a controller to bring the data processing of its app into compliance with the GDPR. In violation of the privacy by design principle, the controller implemented third-party solutions that processed more data than necessary.

An employee complained that her employer, CI & DI Food, never answered her access request for her Libro Unico del Lavoro extract and badge attendance records, sent by certified email in August 2022. The company said it was a human error because only the legal representative could read the PEC mailbox during the summer holidays. It supplied the data only after the Garante invited it to comply, more than thirteen months later. The Garante found breaches of Articles 12 and 15 GDPR and fined the company EUR 4,000. It dropped the alleged breach of Article 5(1)(a).
The DPA fined Telefonica Espana €1,300,000 for a data breach affecting more than a million people and their data connected to wifi routers.

The DPA fined a remote psychic services provider €250,000 for failure to obtain data subjects' explicit consent prior to the processing of sensitive data in the course of recorded consultation sessions.

The DPA fines a remote psychic services provider €150,000 for failure to obtain data subject's explicit consent prior to the processing of sensitive data as well as breaching the principle of storage limitation.

The DPA reprimanded the Interior Ministry after it failed to reply to an erasure request. The DPA highlighted that a controller must always act on such a request and reply to the data subject, even if the request is unfounded.
Garante issued a reprimanded against a news website since it did not show any information pursuant to Article 13 and 14 GDPR.

The Italian DPA reprimanded a controller after it instructed a Tunisian market research company to perform marketing phone calls as a processor. These marketing calls failed to consider the national opt-out register and were generally unlawful.

The DPA fined the Police Service of Northern Ireland GBP 75,000 (€89,930) for a data breach concerning the disclosure of a database including personal data on 9,483 police officers and staff to a public website.

A complainant said the Ministry of Citizen Protection never answered his request about the lawfulness of processing for the new Greek identity cards. The Authority opened its own examination of the processing, heard the Ministry and the Hellenic Police, and reviewed the data protection impact assessment they produced. It found that the controller breached the information duties of Articles 13 and 14 GDPR and the duty to carry out an impact assessment under Article 35(1) before starting the processing. It fined the Ministry EUR 50,000 for the first and EUR 100,000 for the second, and ordered it to document why data beyond what EU law requires are stored on the card chip and to adjust the processing within six months.
The DPA fined a controller €25,000 for the unlawful recording of its employees’ workspaces and for unlawfully making these recordings available online.
The DPA held that the oral disclosure of a data subject’s personal data by a policeman does not fall within the scope of the GDPR.
The DPA fined a large electricity and utilities company €100,000 for unlawfully processing data without a legal basis.

The DPA ordered a telecommunications operator to provide the data subject with access to their personal data in electronic form. The DPA considered mailing a printout insufficient since the data subject had made the access request electronically.

The Croatian DPA announced 12 new administrative fines totalling EUR 270,700. The largest, EUR 190,000, went to a special hospital in the Rijeka area. Patients' radiology images were irrecoverably lost in July 2019 because no backups existed, and the hospital did not notify the authority within 72 hours. The hospital also had no processor contract, no proper retention periods or legal basis for recording call-centre calls, inadequate transparency information, and did not involve its DPO. The remaining fines concern hotels (cookies) and video surveillance notices.

This is a press release announcing 12 new administrative fines totalling EUR 270,700. Fino's EUR 35,700 matches only one part: nine fines on controllers, mostly shops, for not marking premises under video surveillance. The signs were missing, not visible by the time a person enters the recorded area, or lacked the required information. The legal basis is Article 27 of the national Act implementing the GDPR. The release gives no individual amounts, controller names or reference numbers for these nine cases.

The Italian DPA, Garante, issued a 10,000€ fine to journal publisher after it published a non-anonymised judgement containing personal data of children, violating Article 5 GDPR and the Italian Data Protection Code.

A former employee complained that the company never answered his access request of 7 April 2022 for his payslips and other employment data. The company also ignored two requests for information from the Garante, so the Guardia di Finanza had to serve a further request. The Garante found that the company breached Articles 12(3) and 15 GDPR and Article 157 of the Italian Code. It ordered the company to answer the access request within 30 days and imposed a fine of EUR 5,000, and ordered publication of the decision.

The Italian DPA investigated Sky Italia after 275 complaints, mostly about telemarketing, and a separate complaint about a promotional SMS from the NOW service. It found Sky called numbers registered in the Public Opposition Register, used contact data obtained from third parties without checking valid consent and information, and sent promotional SMS to NOW account holders without consent. The Garante declared the processing unlawful, banned further commercial processing without checks, ordered corrective procedures and fined Sky EUR 842,062. The decision is also published as an ancillary sanction.

The DPA fined a software provider for the health sector €800,000 for a violation of Article 5 GDPR and national data protection law. The provider unlawfully processed patients’ data, collected by doctors and incorrectly assumed the data were anonymized even though data subjects could still be identified.

A member of the Carabinieri complained that the nursing order of Udine, together with other regional nursing orders, researched his profession and employer online and sent a note about his and his wife's repeated access requests and complaints to his military command. The order also failed to give an information notice, had no joint-controller agreement and did not answer his access request. The Garante found the processing unlawful, noting that the order only answered the access request after the dispute was notified. It imposed a fine of EUR 8,000, taking account of the order's small size, and ordered publication of the decision.

The DPA ordered the National Police Board of Finland to erase the personal identifying characteristics regarding a person suspected in an offence, which had been taken and processed unnecessarily and in breach of EU law.
The DPA fined a company €50,000 for unlawfully disclosing personal data in a mediation report, thus violating Article 5(1)(f) and Article 32 GDPR.

The DPA fined a clothing retailer €20,000 for failing to demonstrate that the data subject had consented to commercial advertisements when providing their e-mail address in order to receive a digital receipt for a purchase.

The DPA dismissed the complaint lodged by a representative under Article 80(1) GDPR due to the lack of interest of data subject. Additionally, the website operator was advised to implement appropriate measures regarding the processing activities via Google Analytics.
The DPA ordered a controller to bring the websites’ cookie banners into compliance with the GDPR by adding the reject button within its first layer and changing the colours used.

An employee complained that his employer made him use a fingerprint-based time registration system without voluntary consent and without proper information on storage and retention. The Litigation Chamber found that the employer unlawfully processed biometric data and breached purpose limitation, data minimisation and transparency duties. It calculated the fine under the EDPB 04/2022 guidelines, starting from EUR 2 million, adjusting to EUR 160,000 for company size, then reducing to EUR 45,000 after mitigating factors. The complaints against the system supplier (second respondent) were dismissed.
AEPD fined a children's party venue after it disseminated CCTV footage in social media as part of an intimidation and online criticism againts data subjects, in violation of Article 6(1) GDPR.

A University was fined NOK 150,000 (€12,700) for the lack of technical and organisational measures enabling all its employees and students to access personal data stored in an MS Teams folder. Thus, the university violated Article 24 and Article 32 GDPR.
The DPA fined a controller €3,000 that did not comply with requests for erasure by data subjects and did not comply with a request by the DPA on time under Article 31 GDPR.

The DPA fined an electricity provider €25,000 for the failure to comply with a data subject’s erasure and rectification requests and for continuously sending incorrect invoices to the data subject, thus violating Articles 5, 16 and 17 GDPR.

During a press conference, the National Prosecutor's Office disclosed the name, victim status and health information of a crime victim, taken from a district court judgment, without a legal basis. It did not report the breach to the UODO or notify the victim. The UODO President found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a), 6(1), 9(1), 33(1) and 34(1)-(2) GDPR. He imposed an administrative fine of PLN 85,000 and ordered the Office to notify the victim within 3 days. The decision is not yet final.
The DPA reprimanded an online betting provider for unlawfully placing cookies before users could interact with the website’s cookie banner and for sharing personal data with third parties.

The UODO President was examining a complaint about the processing of the complainant's data and identified a sole trader as the controller. The sole trader ignored repeated written and telephone requests for explanations and did not respond when the fine proceedings were opened. The authority found a breach of the duty to cooperate (Art. 31) and of the duty to give access to information (Art. 58(1)(a) and (e)), treated the second as the more serious, and imposed a fine of PLN 19,644 (about EUR 4,500). The text marks the decision as final (prawomocna).
The DPA reprimanded the Finnish Tax Administration for making it unnecessarily burdensome to submit an access request and ordered it to facilitate the use of a representative for access requests.

The DPA found that a data subject’s consent to the processing of their health data by an insurance broker was not freely given since the consent was a condition for a discount on a mortgage’s interest rate.

Apoteket AB, a Swedish pharmacy chain, used the Meta pixel on its website with the advanced matching function switched on from January 2020 to April 2022. As a result, hashed contact details, national ID numbers and data on purchases of privacy-sensitive products were sent to Meta. Apoteket reported the incident itself after an outsider alerted it. IMY found that Apoteket had not taken appropriate technical and organisational measures under Article 32(1) given the high risks. It rated the infringement as low severity but not minor, and imposed an administrative fine of SEK 37,000,000.

Apohem AB, an online pharmacy, had a Meta pixel on its website with the Automatic Advanced Matching function switched on by mistake. From 15 April 2021 to 26 April 2022 this sent customers' names, contact details, purchase information and IP addresses to Meta, linked to roughly 15,000 people. IMY found that the company had not taken appropriate technical and organisational measures and had no routines to follow up unintended changes in its systems, which breached Article 32(1) GDPR. IMY rated the infringement as low gravity but still imposed an administrative fine of SEK 8,000,000, rejecting a reprimand because the data were privacy-sensitive and the processing carried a high risk.

A customer of a telecommunications company asked for access to his data on 25 January 2022, including who among its employees had accessed it and why. The company asked for clarification, said it could not provide the information, and only gave a satisfactory answer on 28 March 2023, after the Litigation Chamber had opened the case on the merits, about 14 months after the request. The Chamber found a continuing breach of the right of access and imposed an administrative fine of EUR 100,000, treating the breach as of low gravity but caused by serious negligence. A later note says the Market Court partially annulled the decision on 22 January 2025 and reduced the fine to EUR 5,000.
The DPA fined Santander €50,000 for processing a data subject’s personal data for advertisement purposes even after the data subject objected to the respective processing.
The DPA reprimanded a food delivery company for violating Article 44 GDPR by transferring personal data of website users to the USA without any appropriate transfer instrument in place.

ANSPDCP finished an investigation of Ana Hotels SRL in July 2024, started after the company notified a personal data breach. A ransomware attack led to unauthorised disclosure of employees' personal data. The authority found the operator had not put in place appropriate technical and organisational security measures under Article 32 GDPR. It fined the company 39,763.20 lei (about EUR 8,000) and ordered a procedural plan for regular testing of IT systems, continuous logging of access and traffic for at least 30 days, and backups.

The DPA fined a bank PLN 4,053,173 (€928,498.06) and ordered it to notify data subjects of a data breach in accordance with Article 34 GDPR after personal data was erroneously transmitted to another bank.

The DPA held that a website that publishes the salary of public companies' managers rightfully rejected an erasure request, since the publication of this data is necessary for exercising the right of freedom of expression and information.

The Danish DPA reported Vejen Municipality to the police and recommended a fine of DKK 200,000 for inadequate security measures. The case began when the municipality notified a breach after five laptops were stolen. The laptops, used by teachers and pupils, held information about pupils, including pupils with special challenges, and none were encrypted. The investigation showed about 300 other computers in the municipality were also unencrypted. In Denmark fines under the GDPR are decided by the courts, and the update says the city court case ended with the municipality accepting a fine of DKK 200,000.

A DPA issued a decision under Article 66 GDPR, prohibiting Meta from sharing advertisements containing the data subject’s data, including fake-ads, on Facebook and Instagram within Poland for three months.

A DPA issued a decision under Article 66 GDPR, prohibiting Meta from sharing advertisements containing data subject’s data, including the fake-ads, on Facebook and Instagram within Poland for three months.
The DPA fined an energy provider €60,000, after its processor erroneously assigned the data subject to a different company and therefore unlawfully disclosed personal data to that company.
The DPA ordered a controller to answer the data subjects’ access request under Article 15 GDPR regarding the delivery of unsolicited advertising e-mails.

The DPA issued a warning to the operator of a video surveillance system for ignoring an access request by a data subject and failing to cooperate with the DPA. Thus, the controller violated Article 12(1), Article 12(3) and Article 31 GDPR.

The DPA dismissed a data subject’s complaint regarding a claimed violation in the right of access since the controller’s time limit for answering the request has not expired at the time of the complaint.

The DPA held that a real estate company unlawfully processed a data subject’s personal data by contacting him despite his explicit statement in an online advertisement that real estate agents were not welcome. Reliance on legitimate interests under GDPR failed because the data subject’s clear objection outweighed the controller’s commercial interests.
The DPA fined a doctor €15,000 for sending election advertisements to patients in violation of the principles of lawfulness, fairness, and transparency of data processing.

The Dutch DPA fined Uber Technologies Inc. and Uber B.V. EUR 290 million. Uber transferred personal data of European drivers (account, licence, location, photo, payment, ID, and in some cases criminal and medical data) to its servers in the United States without appropriate safeguards under Chapter V GDPR. The AP found that Uber B.V. was the exporter and Uber Technologies Inc. the importer, rejecting Uber's view that drivers themselves made the transfer. Uber stopped using standard contractual clauses from August 2021 and only later relied on the successor to the Privacy Shield. The AP held that a fine was both appropriate and necessary and would have imposed the same amount under its 2019 fine policy rules. Uber announced it would object.
The DPA fined a controller €200,000 after it failed to respond to the DPA's requests for further information, finding that it hindered the investigation in violation of Article 58(1) GDPR.
The DPA fined a controller €80,000 for accessing data from its former employee’s mailbox in order to investigate the suspected disclosure of business secrets.

The DPA fined an energy provider €5,000,000 after it failed to implement adequate measures to ensure GDPR-compliance of its processors. The processors were able to forge contracts with unaware data subjects.

Due to human error, a clinic disclosed personal data of a patient undergoing IVF treatment to another patient. The clinic notified the DPA who found it sufficient and appropriate to reprimand the controller.

The Italian DPA, Garante, issued a reprimanded against INPS (National Social Security Institute) after two data breaches occurred, for delaying the notifications and not taking appropriate security measures, considering them inadequate under GDPR standards.

The health authority ULSS 6 Euganea reported a ransomware attack by two criminal groups on its information systems, which compromised health data of thousands of people. The Garante carried out an inspection and found that no multi-factor authentication was in place for VPN access to the network at the time of the breach. It declared the processing unlawful for breaching the integrity and confidentiality principle and the security obligation. It fined the authority EUR 22,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website.

The DPA found that a car rental company’s disclosure of personal data to law enforcement authorities in connection with a traffic code violation was a data breach. The controller submitted data of a previous customer who was not responsible for the traffic code violation.
After non-compliance with a patient’s request for access to pictures taken before and after their surgery, the DPA fined a doctor €4,000 for a violation of Article 15 GDPR.

The DPA reprimanded a controller for unlawfully keeping an employee's email inbox active for an excessive amount of time after the termination of the employment. According to a case by case assessment a period of three months would have been appropriate.
The DPA fined a school €2,000 and held that it could not rely on Article 6(1)(f) GDPR for monitoring classrooms during school hours via video surveillance.

The DPA fined a controller €180,000 because it lacked a legal basis to transfer data concerning a contested debt to a central solvency register and failed to erase the debt from the data subject's financial records.

The DPA fined a race organiser €15,000 for unlawfully collecting participants' health data related to COVID-19. The organiser failed properly inform the participants and to collect their explicit consent under Article 9(1)(a) GDPR

The Polish DPA was handling a complaint about CCTV monitoring by a sole trader and twice asked the trader for explanations, but received no reply. It then opened separate proceedings of its own motion on the failure to cooperate. The trader also ignored the notice of those proceedings and the request for financial data. The President of UODO found breaches of Articles 31 and 58(1)(a) and (e) GDPR and imposed a fine of PLN 21,827, equal to EUR 5,000. The breach was treated as intentional and no mitigating factors were found.

The DPA fined Glovo (a food delivery company) €15,000 after it failed to act on an access request. The DPA considered the fact irrelevant that the request was not sent to the DPO email address but to a different contact point of the controller.
The DPA fined a fintech company €72,000 after its inadequate measures to verify its customer’s identity enabled fraudsters to take out a loan in the name of an unaware data subject.
The DPA fined a controller €4,000 after it shared the data subject’s name on its Google profile. In addition, it did not provide the data subject with the information set by Article 14 GDPR.

The DPA fined a plastic surgery clinic €10,000 after it unlawfully shared before and after pictures of a data subject on its social media account. The DPA highlighted that the pictures contained health data under Article 9(1) GDPR.

A complainant reported that files with personal data of citizens of the Municipality of Alimos could be accessed by anyone online by changing a number in a URL. The flaw came from a faulty software upgrade by the municipality's processor, and about 900 data subjects were affected, including identity cards and passports. The Authority found breaches of security of processing, of the processor contract requirements, and of the breach notification and communication duties. It fined the municipality EUR 10,000 and EUR 5,000, reprimanded it for Article 25(1), and fined the processor EUR 5,000.

An DPA denied a complaint against a public body under Articles 9 and 77 GDPR, holding that publication of a data subject’s political donation did not violate them because the controller had a lawful basis.

In August 2023 Postel suffered a ransomware attack that exfiltrated, and in some cases made unavailable, files with personal data of about 25,000 people, later published on the dark web. The vulnerability exploited had been reported by the software maker and by the national cybersecurity agency in 2022, but Postel had not updated its systems. The Garante found its security measures inadequate and its breach notification incomplete. It fined Postel EUR 900,000 and ordered an extraordinary vulnerability analysis, a plan to detect and manage vulnerabilities, and detection and response times suited to the risk. This is a newsletter item, not the decision itself.
The DPA reprimanded a school after it shared a student's Covid-19 diagnosis with other students in violation of Article 9 GDPR.
The DPA fined a municipality €4,000 after it unlawfully published the names and evaluations of job applicants on its website.

The Italian DPA opened an investigation after a press article reported that the municipality of Treviso used thermal-camera drones and a citizen reporting app called TrevisoSicura. It found the app processing unlawful: no valid legal basis, inadequate privacy notice, no data processing agreement with the app supplier, and failure to apply data protection by design/default and accountability. It fined the municipality EUR 7,000 and ordered publication of the decision. The complaint about the drones was closed without sanction.

The DPA reprimanded the Finnish Golf Union for failing to implement adequate security measures in its golfing app. The app did not use multi-factor authentication and used people's dates of birth as default passwords.
The DPA fined Vinted UAB €2,385,276 and found that its shadow banning practices violated the principles of fairness and transparency.

The DPA fined Aldi HUF 80,000,000 (€204,000) in connection to its age verification practices when selling alcohol. It found that data subjects could not easily access information and that they could not be asked for an ID when there was no doubt they were over 18.

The DPA found a controller did not obtain valid consent for transcription and subsequent processing of customer service recordings of conversation. The controller should then implement appropriate changes in their processing activities.

AXA Real Estate Investment Managers Iberica S.A. faced a data breach involving information for 143 individuals. Although the USB was encrypted, the password was sent within the same envelope, leading to the loss of both the device and its password.
The DPA found that the CCTV installed for the purpose of crime prevention didn’t automatically exempted a data subject from having access to their data.

Avanza Bank notified IMY of a personal data incident: between 15 November 2019 and 2 June 2021 the Meta pixel's Automatic Advanced Matching and Automatic Events functions, activated by mistake, sent data of roughly 500,000 to 1 million people to Meta, including personal identity numbers, loan amounts and account numbers. Much of it was sent in plain text from logged-in areas. IMY found the bank lacked appropriate security measures, did not follow its own routines and could not detect the transfer, breaching Articles 32(1) and 5(1)(f) GDPR. It imposed an administrative fine of SEK 15,000,000, assessing the seriousness as low within the range for Article 5(1)(f) infringements.

A patient complained that a surgeon never answered her access request for the pre-operative photographs taken before her operation. The surgeon only supplied them 302 days later, after the Garante invited him to comply. The Garante also found that the retention period in his privacy notice was too generic. It declared the processing unlawful, fined him EUR 4,000, ordered him to rewrite the notice within 40 days and ordered publication of the decision. The case against the healthcare facility was closed.

A complainant objected that a ranking list from a preselection test of a public competition, naming admitted and non-admitted candidates, stayed online and indexed by search engines on the Municipality of Nepi's website despite removal requests. The Garante found the list was published from 3 February 2015 to 18 February 2022 without a legal basis. It also found the Municipality had no Article 28 data processing agreement with its web management provider until November 2022. It fined the Municipality EUR 8,000 for the publication and EUR 12,000 for the missing processor agreement, EUR 20,000 in total, and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website. No corrective measures were imposed because the conduct had ceased.

A former employee complained that his employer, TS Food Processing, had not answered his access request for personal data stored on the company PC he used. The company first refused, citing fear of trade secrets being taken, then said the request was too generic. Access was given only after the Garante opened its investigation, about two years late. The Garante found breaches of Articles 12(3) and 15 GDPR, fined the company EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

The Italian Garante examined two proceedings against telecom operator Fastweb, started after many complaints and reports about unwanted promotional calls, use of customer contact data for marketing, weak information notices and late replies to data subject requests. It found that Fastweb failed to check the Public Opposition Register for numbers called after web-sales consent, relied on legitimate interest instead of consent for marketing to customers (including up to 24 months after contract end), gave unclear privacy notices and did not answer rights requests on time. It imposed a fine of EUR 1,000,000 and several corrective orders, including a ban on processing numbers whose marketing consent was collected via websales, a double opt-in system and a rewritten notice and consent form. The decision is also published on the Garante's website.

The Italian DPA learned from public sources that the municipality of Forlì offered the 'Falco – Città protetta' app, letting citizens send reports to the local police, who could check CCTV images and collect the reporter's GPS position and phone number. After an investigation it found unlawful processing both in the video surveillance systems and in the Falco app, including failures on transparency, privacy by design, processor contract, security and the DPIA. It fined the municipality EUR 10,000 for the video surveillance violations and EUR 5,000 for the Falco violations, EUR 15,000 in total, and ordered publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were imposed because the conduct had ended.

The DPA reprimanded a municipality for disclosing a Member of Parliament’s personal data after she publicly complained about speeding fines. The DPA held that the municipality had no legal basis to disclose the data even if the information was already publicly available.
The DPA reprimanded a bus operator for publishing the personal phone numbers of its employees on the company intranet for other employees to access.
The DPA found the controller was in breach of Article 12 GDPR and Article 15 GDPR because it didn’t answer access request within one-month period.

The DPA decided to close the case on unlawful processing of a business e-mail address data, referring to the DPA's expediency requirement. According to the DPA, the case encompassed a broader dispute, not to be solved by the DPA decision.

The DPA declared the controller violated Article 12 GDPR and Article 17 GDPR by failing to answer erasure request in timely manner. No corrective measures were imposed as the controller remedied the breach, deleting the data during the investigation.

A public healthcare facility reported a ransomware attack of 10 February 2022 that encrypted its servers holding data of about 30,000 patients and over 1,100 staff, including health data. The Polish DPA found that the facility had not carried out a risk analysis, had not adequately tested its security measures, and had not notified the data subjects of the breach. It imposed a fine of PLN 40,000 and ordered the facility to notify the affected people within 30 days and to bring its security measures into line within 90 days after a risk analysis. The infringement of security was found to be negligent, while the failure to notify was a conscious decision.
The DPA found that a school can partially refuse to act on an access request filed by the parent of a data subject, if the disclosure of certain data can impair the best interest of the minor.

The DPA found that a bank violated the principle of accuracy when it transferred incorrect information about a data subject’s address to an insolvency registry, preventing the latter from notifying the data subject that a processing occurred. The bank paid a reduced fine of €120,000 in accordance with national law.

An individual (controller) was fined €10,000 for unlawfully publishing the names, addresses, telephone numbers, data concerning health and images of ten data subject on Telegram and YouTube with the aim of encouraging others to make abusive phone calls.

The DPA dismissed a complaint against a newspaper, finding that it was publishing information in the public interest and was thus exempt under national law from certain GDPR provisions. It noted that the exemption applies where there is a close nexus between the personal data published and the public interest - including where special categories of data are involved.
